analysis.one_liner: Replaces traditional Medicare with government-subsidized private insurance plans, including a new prescription drug benefit.
analysis.headline: The bill would have replaced traditional Medicare with subsidized private plans and a new drug benefit, but it never received a committee vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Starting in 2008, this bill would have replaced Medicare's guaranteed, government-run benefit with a system of competing private insurance plans, modeled on the health program offered to federal employees. The government would pay each plan's approved premium directly, seniors would pay a premium of their own that rises with income, and plans would have to cover a list of services including outpatient prescription drugs — something traditional Medicare did not cover in 2003. Low-income seniors under 200% of the poverty line would have their full premium paid if they enrolled in a richer 'high option' plan, while people already on Medicare could make a one-time choice to stay in the old program. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, seniors gaining the most would have been low-income beneficiaries: anyone under 200% of the poverty line enrolling in a high option plan would have had their entire premium paid by the government, and every plan had to include outpatient prescription drugs, which Medicare did not cover at all in 2003. Seniors wanting richer coverage would have had access to high option plans with lower deductibles and an annual out-of-pocket cap. The health insurance industry would have gained the most of any concentrated interest: from 2008 the government would pay private plans' approved premium bids directly, and the bill would make those plans the only payment channel for Medicare for everyone newly eligible.

how_it_helps.text: Adds outpatient prescription drug coverage as a required benefit in every Medicare plan, at a time when traditional Medicare covered no outpatient drugs.
Pays the full premium for qualified low-income beneficiaries (income up to 200% of the poverty line) who enroll in a high option plan, with partial help for other low-income beneficiaries.
Requires high option plans to include stop-loss coverage that caps how much a beneficiary can owe out of pocket in a year, and sets their deductibles and cost-sharing below standard plans.
Spells out a required benefit list — hospital, physician, preventive, hospice, home health, ambulance, lab and imaging, drugs, rehabilitation, and durable equipment — that every plan must cover.
Lets people already on Medicare before 2008 keep their current benefits through a one-time election, so no current beneficiary would have been forced out of traditional Medicare.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the premium payments to private plans and any gap between plan costs and dedicated taxes through general revenue contributions to the new Medicare Trust Fund. Higher-income seniors — those at or above 300% of the poverty line — would pay progressively larger premiums, up to 70% of the plan premium. Traditional Medicare, administered directly by the government at relatively low overhead, would be phased out for new beneficiaries, so the program's cost structure would shift toward private plans' administrative costs and profit margins, paid for out of public money.

drawbacks.text: Starting in 2008, everyone newly eligible for Medicare would receive benefits only through a private Medicare plan; the guaranteed, government-administered traditional Medicare would end for new beneficiaries, with existing beneficiaries facing a one-time, irrevocable choice to stay in the old program.

Beneficiary premiums would rise with income: seniors with income at or above 300% of the poverty line would pay 10% more of the plan premium for each additional 100% of poverty-level income, up to a ceiling of 70% of the premium — a large cost increase for middle- and upper-middle-income retirees.

The bill preempts state laws that conflict with its standards for Medicare plans, and the new trust fund design counts general revenue contributions toward a 'programmatic insolvency' trigger at 40% of net expenditures, which could pressure future benefit cuts or premium increases.

Low-income premium subsidies require enrollment in a high option plan, depend on annual state eligibility determinations, and the bill explicitly frees states from any Medicaid obligation to help pay the subsidy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest appeal was real: in 2003 Medicare had no outpatient drug benefit, and this bill would have added one, plus an out-of-pocket cap and full premium coverage for the lowest-income seniors. But it bought those gains by ending guaranteed traditional Medicare for everyone newly eligible after 2007, converting a defined benefit into a subsidy whose value would depend on private plans' bids, and raising premiums for middle- and upper-income seniors to as much as 70% of the cost of coverage. Whether seniors would have come out ahead would have depended entirely on how generously the government funded the bids and how tightly the Secretary policed plan premiums and benefits — discretion the bill left largely to future administrations. Critics of premium-support designs argued that competition among private plans tends to shift costs and risk onto the oldest and sickest beneficiaries; the bill's protections against that (risk adjustment, anti-favorable-selection review) were untested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to their Health Subcommittees in June 2003, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Lee Terry introduced the Medicare Reform Act of 2003 on June 12, 2003, with six Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees the day it was introduced, and within two weeks both committees had sent it to their Health Subcommittees.
No further action was ever taken: the subcommittee referrals of June 19 and June 24, 2003 were the last entries in its legislative history.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died with it, never having reached a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Medicare stayed exactly as it was, and private insurers did not gain the new Medicare market the bill would have created; seniors also did not get the drug benefit and low-income premium subsidies it offered. Congress ultimately passed a different, narrower Medicare drug bill later in 2003.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Medicare's status quo; insurers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so the bill never faced a partisan test on the floor.

industries.note: The bill makes state-licensed private insurers the exclusive channel for Medicare payments from 2008 onward: the government pays their premium bids directly, and only the plan — not providers under traditional Medicare — is eligible for payment. It locks insurers in as the permanent delivery system for Medicare while also imposing federal benefit and solvency requirements on them, and it removes traditional Medicare, the lower-overhead public alternative, for new beneficiaries.

The bill replaces the established Medicare fee-for-service payment rates with negotiated plan bids and strips out several Medicare+Choice rules, so provider revenue would depend on what private plans bid and pay. Plans gain a new drug and managed-care business; providers lose the certainty of the traditional payment system.

States would take on annual eligibility determinations for low-income premium subsidies, but the bill explicitly frees them from any Medicaid obligation to pay for Medicare cost-sharing or match federal funds for it, shifting that burden to the federal treasury.
